g.passage: For three weeks, Mara had watched Dr. Halloway write the brand-name antibiotic on chart after chart, even though the clinic stocked a generic version that treated the same infections identically at a third of the price. The clients rarely questioned him; most, in fact, thanked him for being so thorough. Mara had assumed at first that he simply didn't know the cheaper option existed. ______ when she finally asked him about it, he smiled and explained that the distributor's quarterly bonus depended on volume, and that "people who love their dogs don't haggle."
g.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Accordingly,
In other words,
For instance,
As it turned out,
g.explanation:
정답 D. 지문에는 여러 정보(브랜드 약 처방, 제네릭의 동일 효과·저가, 고객의 감사, Mara의 처음 추측)가 나열되지만, 마지막 문장과 직접 이어지는 것은 바로 앞 문장의 '처음엔 그가 몰랐다고 생각했다'는 추측 하나뿐이다. 마지막 문장은 그 추측이 틀렸음, 즉 그가 알고도 의도적으로(보너스 때문에) 처방했다는 사실을 드러낸다. 따라서 처음 생각과 다른 실제 사정을 알려 주는 'As it turned out,'이 알맞다.
A(Accordingly)는 결과를 나타내는 말이다. 고객들이 감사했다는 부수적 사실의 결과처럼 보일 수는 있지만, 핵심인 '추측이 뒤집혔다'는 점과는 맞지 않고, 고객의 감사 때문에 의사의 설명이 나온 것도 아니다.
B(In other words)는 앞 내용을 바꿔 말할 때 쓴다. 마지막 문장도 앞 문장처럼 의사의 동기를 다루지만, 추측을 다시 말하는 것이 아니라 뒤집는 내용이므로 논리 관계가 틀렸다.
C(For instance)는 예를 들 때 쓴다. 마지막 문장은 앞 문장의 사례가 아니며, 굳이 따지면 브랜드 약 처방 전반의 예시로 엮일 법한 엉뚱한 연결이다.
g.explanation_en:
The answer is D. The passage gives you several details: the brand-name prescriptions, the identical and cheaper generic, the grateful clients, and Mara's first assumption. Only one of them connects directly to the last sentence: Mara's belief that Dr. Halloway didn't know the generic existed. The final sentence shows that belief was wrong. He knew about it and chose the brand name on purpose, for a bonus. "As it turned out," is the transition that introduces what was really going on after a mistaken assumption.
A ("Accordingly,") signals a result. It might seem to follow from the clients thanking him, but that's a side detail. The clients' gratitude didn't cause his explanation, and this choice misses the main point, which is that Mara's assumption gets overturned.
B ("In other words,") signals a restatement. The last sentence is also about the doctor's motives, but it reverses Mara's assumption instead of restating it.
C ("For instance,") signals an example. The final sentence is not an example of anything in the previous sentence, so this connects it to the wrong idea.
g.design: 짧은 소설 장면에 여러 정보를 나열하고, 마지막 문장이 그중 '처음의 추측' 하나만 뒤집도록 설계했다. 오답은 다음 세 가지로 구성했다. 결과 관계(고객 반응이라는 부수적 사실과 연결됨), 같은 주제를 다루지만 관계가 틀린 바꿔 말하기, 엉뚱한 내용과 이어지는 예시.

c.instruction: 서로 배치되거나 상반된 것처럼 보이는 두 가지 관찰(실험 결과, 사례, 수치)이 제시된 짧은 지문을 만들고, 두 관찰을 종합했을 때 나오는 결론을 마지막 문장에서 올바른 전환어로 연결해야 정답이 되게 하라. 오답 3개는 (1)한쪽 관찰만 반영한 전환어, (2)두 관찰이 상반된다는 점만 보고 단순 대조로 처리한 전환어, (3)종합 결론과 무관한 전환어로 구성하라. 계산이나 복잡한 수치 없이 정성적 진술만으로 구성한다.
c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — University librarian observes department chairs quietly pressuring her to remove published research contradicting their funded laboratory's findings

g.passage: In three weeks of meetings, not one of the department chairs mentioned Dr. Okafor's article by name; when Mara raised it herself, Professor Hale only smiled and asked about the weather in her hometown. Yet each meeting, however it began, drifted toward the same topic: the "outdated holdings" crowding the third-floor stacks, beginning, as it happened, with the very journal volume in which Okafor had challenged the chairs' grant-funded laboratory. ______ Mara understood that the chairs' careful silence about the article was not indifference but the request itself, phrased so that no one could ever be said to have made it.
g.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Taken together,
Even so,
Indeed,
Meanwhile,
g.explanation:
정답 A: 지문에는 상반돼 보이는 두 관찰이 나온다. (1) 학과장들은 논문을 한 번도 직접 언급하지 않는다. (2) 그런데도 대화는 늘 그 논문이 실린 학술지 권호를 '낡은 소장 자료'로 치우는 이야기로 흘러간다. 마지막 문장은 이 두 관찰을 함께 놓고 내린 결론이다. 침묵 자체가 압력이었다는 것이다. 따라서 두 관찰을 종합하는 'Taken together,'가 가장 논리적이다.
B 'Even so,': 두 관찰이 상반된다는 점만 보고 단순 대조로 처리한 오답이다. 결론은 두 번째 관찰을 뒤집지 않고 오히려 그것에 기대고 있으므로 양보·대조 관계가 아니다.
C 'Indeed,': 바로 앞 문장(대화가 해당 권호로 흘러감)만 강조·심화하는 전환어로, 한쪽 관찰만 반영한다. 결론의 핵심은 첫 번째 관찰인 '침묵'에 있으며, 결론은 두 관찰을 합쳐야 나온다.
D 'Meanwhile,': 동시에 일어난 다른 사건을 잇는 시간 전환어다. 마지막 문장은 별개의 사건이 아니라 앞 내용에서 끌어낸 깨달음이므로 종합 결론과 관계가 없다.
g.explanation_en:
Choice A is correct. The passage gives two observations that seem to point in opposite directions. First, the chairs never mention Okafor's article. Second, every meeting still drifts toward clearing out the very volume that contains it. The final sentence draws a conclusion that needs both facts: the silence itself was the pressure. "Taken together," signals that kind of combined conclusion.
B ("Even so,") treats the two observations as a simple contrast. But the conclusion doesn't push back against the previous sentence. It builds on it.
C ("Indeed,") only reinforces the sentence right before it, so it reflects one observation. The conclusion depends just as much on the chairs' silence from the first sentence.
D ("Meanwhile,") marks something happening at the same time. Mara's realization isn't a separate event. It's an inference drawn from what came before.
g.design: I built a fiction scene around two observations that seem to clash: the chairs never mention the article, yet every meeting drifts toward removing the volume that contains it. The last sentence joins them into one conclusion. Each wrong answer matches a recipe type: B is a simple contrast, C reflects only one observation, and D has nothing to do with the conclusion.

c.instruction: 한 문장 안에서 수식어구나 비교 표현이 인접한 명사가 아니라 문장 앞부분의 다른 요소(주어나 앞 문장의 대상)를 가리키도록 설계된 짧은 지문을 만들고, 이 실제 지시 관계를 올바르게 파악해야 정답 전환어를 고를 수 있게 하라. 오답 3개는 (1)인접한 명사를 지시 대상으로 잘못 본 전환어, (2)문법적으로는 자연스럽지만 실제 지시관계와 어긋나는 전환어, (3)전혀 다른 요소를 지시 대상으로 삼은 전환어로 구성하라. 문장은 짧고 단순한 구조를 유지한다.
c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — Wedding photographer discovers studio contracts contain hidden clauses allowing owner to sublicense images to stock agencies without bride consent

g.passage: Lena had photographed forty weddings for Halvorsen Studio, and she believed she understood its standard contract better than the owner who had drafted it. Late one night, she reread the fine print and found clause 14. It gave Halvorsen the right to sublicense every image to stock agencies, and no bride ever had to agree. ______ the man she had dismissed as careless had understood the contract far better than she had.
g.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Similarly,
In reality,
Moreover,
For example,
g.explanation:
첫 문장의 비교 표현 "better than the owner"는 바로 옆 명사(contract, owner)가 아니라 문장 앞부분의 주어 Lena가 계약서를 '더 잘 안다고 믿었다'는 내용과 연결된다. 마지막 문장은 사실은 owner가 Lena보다 계약서를 훨씬 잘 알고 있었다고 말하므로, Lena의 믿음을 뒤집는 'In reality,'가 정답이다.
A(Similarly)는 비교 대상을 가까이 있는 owner로 잘못 읽은 오답이다. 두 사람이 똑같이 계약서를 잘 아는 것처럼 보지만, 실제 관계는 대조이다.
C(Moreover)는 문법적으로는 자연스럽게 정보를 덧붙이는 표현이지만, 마지막 문장은 앞 내용을 더하는 것이 아니라 Lena의 믿음을 반박한다.
D(For example)는 바로 앞의 clause 14를 지시 대상으로 삼은 오답이다. 마지막 문장은 그 조항의 사례가 아니라 누가 계약서를 더 잘 이해했는지에 대한 결론이다.
g.explanation_en:
In the first sentence, the comparison "better than the owner" doesn't attach to the nearby nouns (the contract or the owner). It belongs to the subject, Lena: she *believed* she understood the contract better than the owner did. The last sentence shows the opposite. The owner understood it far better than she did. So the blank needs a transition that sets what was actually true against what Lena believed. "In reality," does exactly that.
Here's why the other choices don't work:
- **Similarly,** reads the comparison as being about the nearby noun "owner," as if both people understood the contract equally well. But the two sentences contrast; they don't show a parallel.
- **Moreover,** fits grammatically, but it adds information. The final sentence doesn't add to Lena's belief. It overturns it.
- **For example,** treats clause 14 as the thing being referred to. But the final sentence isn't an example of that clause. It's a conclusion about who really understood the contract.
g.design: The comparison "better than the owner" belongs to Lena, the sentence's subject, and her mistaken belief, not to a nearby noun. To get the answer, students have to see that the final sentence reverses that belief. Distractor A mistakes the nearby noun "owner" for the referent, C fits grammatically but doesn't match the real relationship, and D treats clause 14 as the referent.

c.instruction: 학술적 소재(연구, 인물, 현상 등)에 대한 3~4문장의 짧은 지문을 만들고, 마지막 문장은 앞 내용 중 특정 목적이나 강조점(예: 결과가 아니라 의도, 수치가 아니라 방향성)에 부합하는 전환어를 골라야 정답이 되게 하라. 오답 3개는 (1)앞 문장의 결과·부수적 사실과는 맞지만 지문의 핵심 강조점과는 어긋나는 전환어, (2)방향은 맞지만 논리관계(원인/대조 등)가 틀린 전환어, (3)전혀 다른 내용과 연결되는 전환어로 구성하라. 지문에 여러 개의 정보가 나열되되 그중 한 가지만 답과 직결되도록 설계한다.
c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A woman at a railway station ticket counter realizes the clerk systematically overcharges foreign passengers while keeping local fares unchanged

g.passage: Marguerite had stood in the queue long enough to watch a dozen tickets change hands. The clerk was slow, and twice he miscounted the change for an elderly farmer, apologizing each time with a flustered smile. Yet when a German couple and, later, two Canadian students reached the window, he quoted fares nearly double those on the posted board, while every local traveler paid exactly the printed price. ______ the inflated fares were no slip of a tired hand: the clerk was choosing whom to cheat.
g.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: Similarly,
Nevertheless,
Evidently,
Meanwhile,
g.explanation:
정답 C(Evidently): 마지막 문장은 앞 문장의 관찰(외국인 승객에게만 두 배 요금을 부르고 현지인은 정가)을 근거로 Marguerite가 내리는 결론이다. 강조점은 결과(비싼 요금) 자체가 아니라 '고의성'이며, '관찰한 증거로 보아 분명히'라는 추론을 나타내는 Evidently가 이 흐름에 맞다.
A(Similarly): 농부에게 거스름돈을 잘못 계산한 실수와 이어 보면 그럴듯해 보인다. 하지만 마지막 문장은 비싼 요금이 실수와 '같은 종류'가 아니라 일부러 한 일이라고 말하므로, 둘을 비슷한 것으로 묶는 전환어는 핵심 강조점과 어긋난다.
B(Nevertheless): 서툰 실수와 고의적 사기 사이에 대비가 있는 것은 맞다. 그러나 바로 앞 문장은 결론을 뒷받침하는 증거이지 결론과 반대되는 내용이 아니므로, 대조를 나타내는 접속어는 논리 관계가 맞지 않는다.
D(Meanwhile): 같은 시간에 일어난 다른 장면을 잇는 말이다. 마지막 문장은 새로운 사건이 아니라 앞 관찰에서 이끌어낸 판단이므로 맞지 않는다.
g.explanation_en:
C (Evidently) is correct. The last sentence is a conclusion Marguerite draws from what she has just seen: foreign travelers are quoted double fares, while every local pays the printed price. The point isn't the high fares themselves but the clerk's intent. "Evidently" signals "judging from this evidence, it is clear that," so it fits.
A (Similarly) is tempting because it seems to connect back to the miscounted change for the farmer. But the final sentence says the overcharges are NOT honest slips like that one. Grouping the two as similar goes against the passage's main point.
B (Nevertheless) picks up on a real contrast between clumsy mistakes and deliberate cheating. However, the sentence right before the blank is evidence that supports the conclusion, not something that works against it. A contrast transition gets the relationship wrong.
D (Meanwhile) introduces a separate event happening at the same time. The final sentence isn't a new event. It's a judgment drawn from the earlier observations.
g.design: The passage lists several facts: the clerk is slow, he makes honest change errors, foreigners pay double, and locals pay the posted price. Only the contrast in fares supports the final conclusion about intent, so the answer must signal an inference about deliberateness. The wrong answers are built on a side fact (Similarly, tied to the honest errors), a correct sense of contrast with the wrong logical relationship (Nevertheless), and an unrelated time link (Meanwhile).

c.instruction: 서로 배치되거나 상반된 것처럼 보이는 두 가지 관찰(실험 결과, 사례, 수치)이 제시된 짧은 지문을 만들고, 두 관찰을 종합했을 때 나오는 결론을 마지막 문장에서 올바른 전환어로 연결해야 정답이 되게 하라. 오답 3개는 (1)한쪽 관찰만 반영한 전환어, (2)두 관찰이 상반된다는 점만 보고 단순 대조로 처리한 전환어, (3)종합 결론과 무관한 전환어로 구성하라. 계산이나 복잡한 수치 없이 정성적 진술만으로 구성한다.
c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — Two former research collaborators encounter each other at a provincial museum opening, maintaining surface cordiality while avoiding their abandoned joint project

g.passage: When Teodor spotted Ines across the main gallery of the provincial museum on opening night, he crossed the room at once, kissed her on both cheeks, and asked warmly about her daughter, her new teaching post, even her elderly cat. Yet in twenty minutes of conversation he never once mentioned the river-sediment survey the two of them had worked on for four years before he left it unfinished. Whenever the talk drifted toward hydrology, he turned to admire a case of bronze brooches. ______ Ines understood that his warmth was no sign that he had forgotten the survey but a carefully built fence around it: the more attentive he was to everything else, the more clearly the abandoned project stood at the center of the evening, untouched.
g.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
options: For instance,
Indeed,
Nevertheless,
Thus,
g.explanation:
정답 D(Thus,): 지문에는 겉보기에 서로 맞지 않는 두 관찰이 나온다. 하나는 테오도르가 이네스의 사생활까지 살갑게 챙긴다는 점이고, 다른 하나는 두 사람의 공동 연구 이야기만은 끝까지 피한다는 점이다. 마지막 문장은 이 두 관찰을 함께 놓고 이끌어 낸 결론이다. 따뜻함 자체가 연구를 둘러친 '울타리'라는 것이다. 따라서 앞의 내용에서 결론을 도출하는 Thus가 알맞다.
A(For instance,): 마지막 문장은 앞 문장의 구체적인 예가 아니라 해석이자 결론이므로 종합 결론과 관계없는 전환어다.
B(Indeed,): 회피라는 한쪽 관찰만 보고 '실제로 더 피했다'는 강조로 읽은 경우다. 하지만 마지막 문장은 회피를 강조하는 데서 그치지 않고, 따뜻함과 회피를 하나로 엮어 해석한다.
C(Nevertheless,): 따뜻함과 회피가 서로 반대라는 점만 보고 단순 대조로 처리한 경우다. 이네스의 깨달음은 두 관찰에도 '불구하고' 생긴 것이 아니라 두 관찰 '때문에' 생긴 것이다.
g.explanation_en:
The correct answer is D, "Thus." The passage gives two observations that seem to pull against each other. First, Teodor is very warm and asks about every part of Ines's life. Second, he carefully avoids their abandoned survey. The last sentence is a conclusion Ines draws from both observations together: his warmth is itself a fence around the project. "Thus" signals a conclusion that follows from what came before, so it fits.
A, "For instance," doesn't work because the final sentence isn't an example of the previous sentence. It's an interpretation.
B, "Indeed," only picks up the avoidance. It reads the last sentence as simply stressing that Teodor avoided the topic, but the sentence actually ties his warmth and his avoidance into one insight.
C, "Nevertheless," treats the two observations as a plain contrast. Ines doesn't reach her conclusion in spite of what she saw. She reaches it because of what she saw.
g.design: The two observations, warm attentiveness and careful avoidance, look contradictory, and the final sentence combines them into one conclusion. The wrong answers follow the recipe: one reflects only one observation (Indeed), one treats the observations as a simple contrast (Nevertheless), and one has nothing to do with the conclusion (For instance).

c.instruction:
- easy: 한 가지 명시적 개념·규칙만으로 푼다. 단서가 지문에 직접 드러나고 추론은 한 단계 이하이다. 어휘·문장은 평이하다. 오답 3개는 해당 규칙을 알면 바로 배제되지만 규칙을 모르는 학생에게는 그럴듯해 보이는 전형적 오개념이어야 한다(말도 안 되는 선택지 금지).
- 세부 기술 힌트: 수식어가 짧은 주어-동사 수 일치, 시제 일관성, 대명사 격/수 일치처럼 한 규칙을 묻는 문제.
c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A translator working alone discovers her client deliberately mistranslated contract terms in previous drafts she must now correct and resubmit

g.passage: Alone in her small apartment, Mira spread the earlier drafts of the contract across her kitchen table. Comparing them line by line, she saw the pattern at once. The clause about payment ______ been changed in every version her client had sent: "thirty days" had quietly become "ninety." Sighing, she reached for a red pen and began the translation again.
g.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: had
having
to have
have
g.design: Tests one rule only: the sentence needs a finite main verb for the subject "The clause." The short modifier "about payment" sits between subject and verb, and the past tense matches the surrounding narration.
g.explanation: 이 문장의 주어는 단수 "The clause"이며, "about payment"는 주어를 꾸미는 짧은 수식어일 뿐이므로 문장에는 정형 동사가 필요하다. A의 "had"는 단수 주어에 맞고, 과거로 서술되는 지문의 시제와도 맞는 과거완료를 만든다. B의 "having"과 C의 "to have"는 정형 동사가 아니어서 문장에 본동사가 없게 된다. D의 "have"는 복수 주어에 쓰는 형태로, 바로 앞의 "payment"나 복수인 "drafts"에 끌려 고르기 쉽지만 단수 주어 "clause"와 수가 맞지 않는다.
g.explanation_en: The subject of this sentence is the singular noun "The clause." The phrase "about payment" just describes it, so the sentence still needs a finite main verb. A, "had," works with a singular subject and forms the past perfect, which fits the past-tense narration. B, "having," and C, "to have," aren't finite verbs, so with either one the sentence has no main verb. D, "have," is the plural form. You might pick it if you're thinking of "drafts" or the nearby word "payment," but it doesn't agree with the singular subject "clause."

c.instruction:
- easy: 한 가지 명시적 개념·규칙만으로 푼다. 단서가 지문에 직접 드러나고 추론은 한 단계 이하이다. 어휘·문장은 평이하다. 오답 3개는 해당 규칙을 알면 바로 배제되지만 규칙을 모르는 학생에게는 그럴듯해 보이는 전형적 오개념이어야 한다(말도 안 되는 선택지 금지).
- 세부 기술 힌트: 수식어가 짧은 주어-동사 수 일치, 시제 일관성, 대명사 격/수 일치처럼 한 규칙을 묻는 문제.
c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A lighthouse keeper documents a shipping company vessel repeatedly entering restricted waters despite posted warning signs in his logbook

g.passage: Every evening, Tomas opened his logbook and wrote down what he had seen from the lamp room. For the third time that week, the gray freighter had steamed straight into the shallow channel. The warning signs on the northern rocks ______ clearly that ships must stay out, yet the vessel never slowed. Tomas pressed his pen hard into the page and recorded the time: 6:42 p.m.
g.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: states
state
is stating
has stated
g.design: 수식어(on the northern rocks)가 짧은 복수 주어 'signs'와 동사의 수 일치라는 단일 규칙만 묻는다. 오답은 모두 바로 앞의 단수 명사 'rocks'가 아니라 단수 주어로 착각할 때 고르게 되는 단수형이다.
g.explanation: 이 문장의 주어는 복수 명사 'signs'이고, 'on the northern rocks'는 주어를 꾸미는 수식어일 뿐이다. 따라서 동사도 복수형이어야 하므로 B의 'state'가 정답이다. A의 'states'는 단수 동사라서 복수 주어와 맞지 않는다. C의 'is stating'과 D의 'has stated'도 단수 조동사(is, has)를 쓰므로 수 일치 규칙에 어긋난다.
g.explanation_en: The subject of this sentence is the plural noun "signs"; the phrase "on the northern rocks" just describes those signs. A plural subject needs a plural verb, so B, "state," is correct. A, "states," is a singular verb, so it doesn't agree with "signs." C, "is stating," and D, "has stated," also use singular helping verbs ("is" and "has"), so they break subject-verb agreement too.

g.explanation_en: The subject of this sentence is the singular noun "the bow arm"; the phrase "of her most promising student" only modifies that subject. So the verb has to be singular, and C, "trembles," is the correct answer because it is singular and also matches the present tense of "climbs." A, B, and D are all verb forms used with plural subjects, so they don't agree with the singular subject "arm." These wrong answers are easy to pick if you mistake a nearby word for the subject.

c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A cartographer discovers her publisher altered territorial boundary lines on maps without consulting her original source materials or permission

g.passage:
The following text is adapted from a novel. Ines Varga, a cartographer, has just received the printed edition of her atlas of the river provinces.

Ines turned to plate fourteen and stopped. The border between Halden and the eastern marshes no longer followed the old riverbed she had traced from the 1841 survey; it now bent west, swallowing three villages. She had not drawn that line. Her editor, Mr. Corbin, insisted over the telephone that the change was a "routine correction" made by the engraver to match a newer government chart. But Ines suspected otherwise: she believed the publisher had moved the line deliberately, without ever looking at her survey notes, to suit the atlas's buyers in Halden.
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ines's suspicion about the altered border?
options: The engraver who prepared plate fourteen had worked for the publisher for many years and had altered plates in earlier atlases at the editor's request.
A newer government chart of the region exists, and on it the border between Halden and the eastern marshes follows a course slightly different from the 1841 survey.
Ines's survey notes, including her tracings of the 1841 riverbed, were stored in the publisher's archive throughout the period when plate fourteen was being engraved.

The publisher's records show that Ines's survey notes were never removed from their sealed archive box, and a letter from Mr. Corbin to a Halden bookseller promises that the new edition will "show Halden as its readers expect."
g.explanation: 이네스의 의심은 두 부분으로 이루어진다. 출판사가 그녀의 조사 노트를 보지 않았다는 것, 그리고 할든 구매자들에게 맞추려고 국경선을 의도적으로 옮겼다는 것이다. D는 노트가 봉인된 상자에서 한 번도 꺼내지지 않았다는 기록과 할든 독자의 기대에 맞추겠다는 편지를 함께 제시하므로 두 부분을 모두 직접 뒷받침한다. A는 판각공이 예전에도 판을 수정한 적이 있다는 것만 보여 줄 뿐, 이번 수정의 동기나 노트를 보지 않았다는 점은 입증하지 못한다. B는 오히려 코빈의 '통상적 정정' 해명을 지지하며, C는 노트가 출판사 안에 있었다는 사실만 말할 뿐 실제로 참고했는지는 알려 주지 않는다.
g.explanation_en: Ines's suspicion has two parts: the publisher never looked at her survey notes, and it moved the line on purpose to please buyers in Halden. Choice D supports both parts directly, since the notes were never taken out of their sealed box and Corbin's letter promises to show Halden "as its readers expect." Choice A only tells you the engraver had changed plates before; it shows neither the motive for this change nor that her notes were ignored. Choice B actually backs Corbin's claim that the edit was a "routine correction" based on a newer chart. Choice C only says the notes were at the publisher's office, which doesn't tell you whether anyone ignored them or consulted them.
g.design: To get this right, students must connect both parts of the suspicion (the notes were ignored and the change served a motive). Choices A and C each sound related to only part of it, and B supports the opposing explanation.

g.passage: In Delia Harrow's novel The Sorting Room, Wilma Ostrander, a retired postal clerk, attends a county meeting about a plan to close the rural mail sorting facility in Fenwick Hollow, where she worked for thirty-two years. Wilma sits in the back row and says little while officials present charts on cost savings. Some readers see her silent anger as grief for her own working life. Literary scholar Tomas Reyes argues instead that Wilma's opposition is mainly about the town, not about herself: she believes the facility's workers kept track of neighbors' needs in ways that no regional center could.
g.question: Which finding about the novel, if true, would most directly support Reyes's interpretation?
options: In a later scene, Wilma tells an official that the Fenwick clerks always knew which elderly residents had stopped collecting their letters and would send someone to check on them.
In a later scene, Wilma takes her old facility badge from a kitchen drawer after the meeting and holds it for a long time without speaking.
In a later scene, Wilma tells the officials that she gave thirty-two years to the facility and deserves more respect than a chart of numbers.
In a later scene, several Fenwick residents complain to Wilma that their packages will take longer to arrive once mail is sorted elsewhere.
g.explanation: Reyes는 Wilma의 반대가 자신의 과거에 대한 슬픔보다는 시설 직원들이 이웃의 필요를 살폈다는 공동체적 이유에서 나온다고 본다. A는 Wilma가 직원들이 편지를 찾아가지 않는 노인을 알아채고 사람을 보내 확인했다고 말하는 장면이므로, 그녀의 관심이 마을 사람들의 안녕에 있음을 직접 보여 준다. B는 지난 직장 생활에 대한 개인적 그리움을 보여 주므로 오히려 Reyes가 반박하는 해석에 가깝다. C도 Wilma가 반대 의견을 말하기는 하지만 그 근거가 자신의 근속 기간과 존중받고 싶은 마음이라 개인적 동기를 드러낸다. D는 공동체가 입는 피해를 다루지만 불만을 말하는 사람이 다른 주민들이고 내용도 배송 속도뿐이어서 Wilma 자신의 동기나 이웃을 살피는 일에 대해서는 보여 주는 것이 없다.
g.explanation_en: Reyes claims that Wilma opposes the closure mainly because of what the town would lose, since the facility's workers kept track of neighbors' needs, and not because she is grieving her own career. Choice A shows Wilma pointing out that the clerks noticed when elderly residents stopped collecting their letters and sent someone to check on them, so it shows directly that her concern is for the community. Choice B shows private nostalgia for her working life, which fits the reading Reyes rejects. In choice C, Wilma does speak against the plan, but her reason is her own years of service and her wish for respect, so her motive is personal. Choice D is about harm to the town, but the complaint comes from other residents and only concerns delivery speed, so it tells you nothing about Wilma's motive or about neighbors looking out for one another.
g.design: Every option uses the same "In a later scene" frame and is tied to the meeting. C (Wilma speaks against the plan) and D (harm to the community) each match part of the claim, so a skimming reader could pick them. Only A shows both Wilma's own motive and its community-centered nature, and the question avoids A's key words.

The following text is adapted from a short story. Ilse Varga, a bookbinder, has just learned that her apprentice, Tomas, has been secretly selling her volumes to a rival shop across the river.

The books lay on the rival's counter in a neat stack, and Ilse knew them at once: her goatskin, her marbled endpapers. But the spines were bare of lettering, the headbands were missing, and on one the boards still showed pencil marks where she had meant to tool a border. "He let you have them like this," she said. The rival shrugged. "Cheaply, too." Ilse ran her thumb along an untrimmed edge and said nothing more.

A literary critic argues that Ilse is troubled less by the money she has lost than by the idea that work she had not finished is now out in the world, representing her craft.
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the critic's interpretation?
options: Later in the story, Ilse sits up all night going through her ledger, adding up the sum she would have earned had the volumes been sold at her usual price.
Later in the story, Tomas gives Ilse every coin he received from the rival, but she will not speak to him until the volumes are bought back and completed at her bench.
Later in the story, customers at the rival's shop are described as admiring the fine goatskin and marbled endpapers of the volumes Tomas sold.
Later in the story, Ilse remembers that as a young apprentice she once sold a few scraps of leather from her own master's workshop without permission.
g.explanation: 비평가의 주장은 일세가 잃은 돈보다 미완성 작품이 자신의 솜씨를 대표하게 된 점에 더 괴로워한다는 것이다. B에서는 돈을 모두 돌려받았는데도 책이 회수되어 완성될 때까지 화가 풀리지 않으므로, 돈이 아니라 미완성 상태가 핵심 문제임을 보여 준다. A는 일세가 잃은 수입에 매달리는 모습이므로 오히려 주장을 약화한다. C는 책의 품질에 대한 손님들의 반응일 뿐 일세의 감정을 드러내지 않는다. D는 도제 시절의 비슷한 잘못을 떠올리는 장면으로, 그녀가 무엇 때문에 괴로워하는지와는 관련이 없다.
g.explanation_en: The critic claims Ilse cares less about the lost money than about her unfinished work standing for her craft in public. In B, Ilse gets all the money back and is still angry until the books are recovered and finished, which shows that the unfinished state, not the income, is what bothers her. A shows her focused on lost earnings, so it would actually weaken the claim. C describes how customers react to the books' materials and tells you nothing about Ilse's feelings. D brings up a similar mistake from her past, but it doesn't show what is troubling her now.
g.design: To answer correctly, you have to link the critic's money-versus-unfinished-work contrast to a finding that separates the two (money returned, anger stays). The distractors pick up surface details of the scene, such as the ledger, the materials, and an apprentice's wrongdoing.

g.passage:
The following text is adapted from a novel. Inés Varga, a meteorologist, has just presented flood-risk projections to a city planning board.

Inés clicked to the final map, where the riverside parcels glowed red, and waited. No one asked about the hundred-year floodplain or the storm-surge models she had spent the winter refining. The chair thanked her warmly, the way one thanks a child for a recital, and moved to the vote. Seven hands rose to approve the Harbor Commons towers. Driving home, Inés replayed the meeting. The board members had not looked confused or skeptical while she spoke; they had not looked at the screen at all. She began to suspect that her presentation had never been part of the decision—that the outcome had been fixed before she ever walked into the room.
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Inés's suspicion?
options: The board's internal notes showed that several members privately agreed that the riverside parcels faced serious flood risk.
The board's financial records showed that the developer of Harbor Commons had contributed to the campaigns of most board members.
The board's approval paperwork showed that every member's endorsement of Harbor Commons had been recorded three days before the meeting.
The board's archives showed that members had approved projects in other flood-prone areas despite earlier warnings from consultants.
g.explanation: 이네스의 의심은 회의 전에 이미 결과가 정해져 있었다는 것, 즉 시점에 관한 것이다. C는 회의 사흘 전에 모든 위원의 찬성이 이미 기록되어 있었음을 보여 주므로 그녀의 발표가 결정에 관여할 수 없었다는 점을 직접 뒷받침한다. A는 위원들이 위험을 알고도 무시했다는 점은 보여 주지만, 결정이 미리 내려졌는지는 보여 주지 않는다. B는 찬성할 동기를 제시할 뿐 결정 시점은 입증하지 못하며, D는 과거의 행동 패턴일 뿐 이번 투표가 사전에 확정되었다는 증거는 아니다.
g.explanation_en: Inés's suspicion is about timing: she thinks the outcome was settled before she presented. C shows that every member's endorsement had already been recorded three days before the meeting, so it directly supports the idea that her presentation never played a part in the decision. A shows that members knew about the risk and ignored it anyway, but it doesn't show that the decision was made ahead of time. B gives a possible motive for approving the project, not evidence of when the decision was made, and D describes a past pattern rather than showing that this particular vote was fixed in advance.
g.design: To answer correctly, students first have to see that the suspicion is specifically about the decision being made in advance, and then pick the only finding that addresses that timing. The distractors offer partial support through knowledge of the risk, a motive, and past behavior.

The following text is from a short story. Ines, a dental hygienist, is setting up a treatment room.

Ines was laying out the scalers in their usual order when Dr. Pruett's voice came through the thin wall. "Put Mr. Adeyemi down for four crowns," he told the receptionist. "Upper left. Tell him it can't wait." Ines had cleaned Mr. Adeyemi's teeth only last week. She remembered a shallow stain on one molar and nothing more. She set down the mirror and pictured his radiographs, the pale outlines she had studied under the light. But she read films for tartar, she reminded herself, not for decay; she was not the one with the degree. She picked up the scalers and lined them up again, though they had been straight the first time.

A literary critic argues that Ines stays silent in this scene mainly because she doubts what she herself observed, not because she fears what might happen to her if she speaks up.
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the critic's argument?
options: Earlier in the story, Ines worries that her rent is going up and notes that Dr. Pruett's clinic is the only dental office in her small town that is hiring.
Later in the story, Ines tells her sister that Dr. Pruett once fired an assistant who questioned one of his treatment plans in front of a patient.
Later in the story, Ines looks at Mr. Adeyemi's radiographs again and notices the same shallow stain on the molar that she remembered from the cleaning.
Later in the story, Ines confronts Dr. Pruett only after a dentist at another clinic looks at the same radiographs and confirms that the teeth show no decay.
g.explanation: 비평가는 Ines의 침묵이 자기 관찰에 대한 불신 때문이며, 보복에 대한 두려움 때문이 아니라고 주장한다. D는 다른 치과의사가 그녀의 관찰을 확인해 주자마자 Ines가 위험을 무릅쓰고 맞선다는 점을 보여 준다. 따라서 그녀를 막고 있던 것은 두려움이 아니라 자기 판단에 대한 의심이었다는 뜻이 된다. A와 B는 경제적 불안과 해고 위험을 부각하므로 오히려 '두려움' 해석을 뒷받침한다. C는 Ines의 관찰이 맞았음을 보여 줄 뿐, 그녀가 왜 침묵했는지는 설명하지 못한다.
g.explanation_en: The critic argues that Ines stays quiet because she doubts her own observations, not because she fears consequences. D shows that Ines confronts Dr. Pruett as soon as another dentist confirms what she saw, even though speaking up is still risky. That means doubt about her own judgment, not fear, was what held her back. A and B point to money worries and the risk of being fired, so they actually support the fear explanation the critic rejects. C shows that Ines's observation was accurate, but it says nothing about why she stayed silent.
g.design: To answer, students must connect the critic's two-part claim (self-doubt, not fear) to a finding that both points to self-doubt and rules out fear. Two distractors are about Ines's motives but support the rejected explanation, and C repeats details from the scene without explaining why she stayed silent.

c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A swimming pool maintenance worker observes the facility manager falsifying chemical safety test results on official documentation sheets regularly

g.passage:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Teodoro cleans the pools at a municipal aquatic center, where the manager, Mr. Halvorsen, records the daily chlorine and pH readings.

Every morning Teodoro dipped the test strips himself, and every morning he watched them bloom the wrong color: pale where they should have been deep, the chlorine thin as a rumor. Then he would pass the office and see Halvorsen bent over the clipboard, writing the same tidy numbers he had written the day before. Teodoro told his sister that the manager was not careless but frightened—that Halvorsen invented the figures because he believed an honest report would cost him his job, not because he didn't understand what the strips meant.
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Teodoro's interpretation of Halvorsen's behavior?
options: Halvorsen keeps a private notebook in his desk listing the true readings beside a note reading "If the county sees these, they replace me."
Halvorsen keeps a private notebook in his desk listing the readings he recorded, each copied neatly from the previous day's sheet.
Halvorsen keeps a private notebook in his desk listing the dates when the county last inspected the pool and found it acceptable.
Halvorsen keeps a private notebook in his desk listing the chlorine levels he believes are standard, several of which are well below the safe range.
g.design: 테오도로의 해석은 두 부분(Halvorsen이 진짜 수치의 의미를 안다 + 해고가 두려워 조작한다)으로 되어 있어, 둘 다 뒷받침하는 발견을 골라야 한다. 오답은 모두 같은 문장 틀을 쓰고, 각각 조작 사실만 보여 주거나 무관한 맥락을 제시하거나 오히려 해석을 약화한다.
g.explanation: 테오도로는 Halvorsen이 수치의 의미를 이해하면서도 정직하게 보고하면 직장을 잃을까 두려워 수치를 꾸며낸다고 해석한다. A는 그가 실제 수치를 알고 있다는 점과 교체될까 두려워한다는 점을 함께 보여 주므로 해석의 두 부분을 모두 뒷받침한다. B는 조작 사실만 확인해 줄 뿐 동기는 보여 주지 못한다. C는 점검 기록일 뿐 두려움이나 이해 여부와 직접 연결되지 않는다. D는 Halvorsen이 안전 기준을 잘못 알고 있음을 시사하므로 '이해 부족이 아니다'라는 해석을 오히려 약화한다.
g.explanation_en: Teodoro's interpretation has two parts: Halvorsen understands what the readings mean, and he fakes them because he's afraid an honest report will cost him his job. Choice A supports both parts, since it shows he knows the true readings and fears being replaced. Choice B confirms only that he copies the numbers, which tells you nothing about why. Choice C records past inspections, but that has no direct connection to fear or understanding. Choice D suggests he misunderstands the safe levels, which actually weakens Teodoro's claim that ignorance isn't the cause.

c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A rural schoolteacher watches administrators systematically discourage low-income students from enrolling in advanced placement courses during registration week

g.passage:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Delia Harlan teaches eighth-grade English in a farming county and has been asked to help at the high school during registration week.

Delia sat at the folding table beside Mr. Pruitt, the assistant principal, and watched the line move. When the Callahan girl asked for AP Chemistry, Pruitt tapped her free-lunch form and said, kindly enough, that the course was "a lot of after-school lab time, and you've got the bus to think about." The girl took regular chemistry instead. An hour later, the dentist's son asked for the same class and got it with a nod. Pruitt would have said that he simply knew which students were ready. But Delia had graded both of those students' essays two years before, and she did not believe that readiness was what he was sorting by. She suspected that what decided who got steered away was the family's money, not the student's record.
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Delia's suspicion?
options: Students who qualified for free lunch made up a smaller share of the AP Chemistry roster than of the school's incoming class as a whole.
Among students with the same prior grades and placement-test scores, those who qualified for free lunch were advised out of AP courses far more often than those who did not.
Students with higher placement-test scores were much more likely to be enrolled in AP courses than students with lower scores were.
Students who rode the bus to school were advised out of AP courses more often than students who were driven to school by a parent.
g.explanation:
Delia은 학생의 성적(준비도)이 아니라 가정의 경제력이 AP 수강 만류를 결정한다고 의심한다. 이를 뒷받침하려면 두 변수, 즉 소득과 학업 성적을 함께 봐야 한다. B는 성적을 같게 맞춘 상태에서도 무료 급식 대상 학생이 훨씬 자주 만류되었다는 결과이므로, Pruitt의 '준비도' 설명을 배제하고 소득의 효과만 따로 보여 준다. 그래서 B가 정답이다.
A(소득 변수만 봄): 저소득 학생이 AP에 적게 들어갔다는 사실은 성적 차이로도 설명할 수 있어서, Pruitt의 설명을 배제하지 못한다.
C(성적 변수만 봄): 성적이 수강을 좌우한다는 결과이므로 오히려 Pruitt의 입장에 가깝고, 소득에 대해서는 아무것도 말해 주지 않는다.
D(제3의 변수): 통학 버스 이용 여부는 자료에 없는 별개의 변수이다. 소득과 관련이 있을 수는 있지만 소득과 같지 않고, 성적을 통제하지도 않았다.
g.explanation_en:
Delia suspects that family income, not a student's academic record, decides who is steered away from AP courses. To support that, a finding has to look at both variables together. Choice B holds prior grades and test scores constant and still shows that students who qualified for free lunch were advised out far more often. That rules out Pruitt's "readiness" explanation and isolates income, so B is correct.
A looks only at income. Low-income students could be underrepresented in AP because of differences in their records, so A doesn't rule out Pruitt's explanation.
C looks only at academic record. It actually fits Pruitt's claim, and it says nothing about income.
D brings in a third variable, bus riding, that the claim isn't about. Bus riding may be related to income, but it isn't the same thing, and this finding doesn't control for academic record either.
g.design: To support the claim, students have to combine two variables: income and academic record. B controls for record and still shows an income effect. A uses only income, C uses only record, and D swaps in a third variable, bus riding.

c.instruction: 지문에 상관관계나 동시 발생 사실만 제시하고, 이를 근거로 특정 가설(주장)의 인과성을 지지하는지 판단해야 하는 문항을 만들어라. 정답은 인과 방향과 대안 설명 가능성을 함께 고려해 타당하게 지지하는 것이어야 하고, 오답 3개는 각각 '상관을 그대로 인과로 오해', '인과 방향을 반대로 설정', '무관한 제3의 원인을 인과로 제시'로 구성하라.
c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A film projectionist at an independent cinema discovers the distribution company has been billing them for incomplete reels of movies

g.passage:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Mara is the only projectionist at the Lantern, a small independent cinema.

Mara threaded the last reel and stopped. The can was labeled six of six, but the story had jumped from the train station straight to the funeral. It was the third short print since March, and each time the invoice had charged for a complete film. She spread the shipping slips across the rewind bench. March was the month the distributor began routing the Lantern's prints through its new depot in Ashford, and every short print had arrived with an Ashford stamp. "Somebody in Ashford is pulling reels," she told the manager, "and we're paying for what they keep."
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mara's suspicion?
options: Of all the prints the Lantern received since March, every one that was missing a reel carried an Ashford depot stamp on its shipping slip.
The distributor opened the Ashford depot in March after other cinemas had complained that their prints were arriving with reels missing.
Since March, prints the distributor sent to the Lantern directly from its main warehouse arrived complete, while prints of the same films routed through Ashford arrived short.
In March, the distributor also replaced its sturdy metal film cans with lighter cans whose lids can slip open during shipping.
g.explanation:
정답 C: 같은 시기·같은 영화인데 배송 경로(Ashford 경유 여부)만 다를 때 결과가 갈리므로, 시기나 영화 자체 같은 다른 요인을 통제하고 Ashford가 원인이라는 추론을 직접 지지한다.
A: 지문에 이미 나온 상관관계(누락 필름에 모두 Ashford 도장)를 다시 말할 뿐이다. 3월 이후 모든 필름이 Ashford를 거쳤다면 도장은 아무것도 구별하지 못한다. 상관을 인과로 착각한 오답이다.
B: 릴 누락 문제가 Ashford 개설의 원인이 되었다는 내용으로, 인과 방향이 거꾸로다. 게다가 누락이 Ashford 이전부터 있었음을 시사하므로 오히려 Mara의 의심을 약화한다.
D: 같은 달에 바뀐 다른 요인(뚜껑이 쉽게 열리는 깡통)을 제시한다. 이는 Ashford 직원의 소행이 아닌 대안적 설명이 되므로 Mara의 주장을 지지하지 못한다.
g.explanation_en:
Choice C is the best answer. It compares prints of the same films shipped during the same months. The only difference between them is whether they went through Ashford. Because the short prints line up with that one difference, timing and the films themselves are ruled out, and Ashford is singled out as the cause.
Choice A only repeats the correlation the passage already gives. If every print since March went through Ashford, an Ashford stamp on the short ones tells you nothing new. This choice treats correlation as causation.
Choice B reverses the direction of cause: missing reels led to the depot being opened. It also suggests prints were already coming up short before Ashford existed, which weakens Mara's suspicion.
Choice D gives a different change that happened in the same month, new cans whose lids can slip open. That offers another explanation for the lost reels, so it doesn't support the claim that someone in Ashford is taking them.
g.design: The passage gives only a timing-and-stamp correlation. The correct answer is a controlled comparison: same films, same period, different shipping route. The wrong answers restate the correlation (A), reverse the causal direction (B), and offer a third factor from the same month (D).

c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A geological surveyor's environmental impact assessment is quietly shelved after developers directly lobby the regional planning authority to ignore it

g.passage:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Imelda Varga, a geological surveyor, has submitted a report warning that the limestone beneath a proposed housing site is riddled with sinkholes.

Three weeks after she filed the report, Imelda rode the elevator up to the regional planning office and found the receptionist unwilling to look at her. Her assessment, she was told, was "still under review." On the drive home she ran through the possibilities. The board might simply be overworked; reports of hers had sat for months before. But she kept thinking of the Calloway Group's executives, whom she had passed in the lobby that morning, laughing with the board chair. Imelda became convinced that the delay was no accident: the developers, she believed, had persuaded the board to bury her findings so that construction could begin before anyone read them.
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Imelda's belief about why her assessment has not been acted on?
options: Board records show that the limestone formations Imelda surveyed also extend beneath several farms outside the proposed housing site.
Board records show that every environmental report filed that quarter, including those unrelated to any Calloway project, was delayed by a similar length of time.
Board records show that Calloway Group executives visited the planning office on the same morning Imelda went to ask about her report.
Board records show that, after a private meeting with Calloway representatives, the chair ordered staff to remove Imelda's report from the agenda and approved the building permits.
g.explanation:
Imelda의 믿음은 '개발업자가 위원회를 설득해 보고서를 묻어버렸고, 그 목적은 공사를 먼저 시작하는 것'이라는 인과 주장이다. D는 Calloway와의 비공개 회의 → 위원장의 보고서 의제 제외 지시 → 허가 승인이라는 순서를 보여 주어, 로비가 보고서 보류로 이어졌고 개발이 진행되었다는 인과 연결을 직접 입증한다.
A: 석회암 지층이 농장 아래까지 뻗어 있다는 사실은 지질학적 사실일 뿐, 보고서가 왜 보류되었는지와는 무관하다.
B: 관련 없는 보고서까지 모두 비슷하게 지연되었다면 '위원회가 그저 업무 과다'라는 다른 설명을 뒷받침하므로 Imelda의 믿음을 오히려 약화한다.
C: 임원들이 그날 아침 사무실에 있었다는 것은 지문에 이미 나온 내용(로비에서 마주침)을 다시 말한 것일 뿐, 이들이 보고서 보류에 영향을 주었다는 새로운 증거가 아니다.
g.explanation_en:
Imelda's belief is a causal claim: the developers persuaded the board to bury her report so that construction could go ahead. D gives you the whole chain in order: a private meeting with Calloway, then the chair's order to pull her report from the agenda, then approval of the permits. That ties the lobbying directly to the shelving and to the outcome she predicted.
A is wrong because it's a geological fact about how far the limestone extends. It says nothing about why the report was delayed.
B is wrong because if unrelated reports were delayed just as long, that points to the board simply being overworked, the innocent explanation Imelda considered. So B weakens her belief.
C is wrong because it only repeats what the passage already tells you: she saw the executives in the lobby that morning. Being in the building doesn't show that they influenced what happened to her report.
g.design: 지문은 가설(로비→보고서 매장)만 제시하고, 정답은 인과 고리 전체를 채우는 가상의 기록이다. 오답은 무관한 사실(A), 반박하는 결과(B), 지문에 이미 있는 사실의 재진술(C)로 구성했으며 네 선택지 모두 'Board records show that...'이라는 같은 문장 틀을 쓴다.

c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A textile conservator notices colleagues reattaching fragile museum tapestries using adhesives explicitly forbidden by professional conservation ethics guidelines

g.passage:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Ines, a textile conservator at a city museum, has found traces of a synthetic heat-set adhesive on the backs of several tapestries. Professional conservation ethics guidelines forbid this adhesive because it cannot be fully removed later.

Ines spread her notebook across the worktable. For three weeks she had been recording every tapestry that came off the repair frames: its fibers, its date of departure for loan, and what she found when she turned it over. She did not think her colleagues were careless. Stitching a torn silk warp back onto its linen support could take a month of patient needlework, while wool, being sturdier, could be stitched far more quickly. And a piece that would not leave the building until next year gave everyone time. "They reach for the glue," she said quietly to the empty studio, "only when the silk and the calendar are both against them."
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ines's suspicion?
options: Almost every tapestry with adhesive residue in Ines's notebook had silk warps and was due to be shipped within a month, while silk-warped tapestries with later departure dates had been repaired only by stitching.
Almost every tapestry with adhesive residue in Ines's notebook had silk warps, while silk-warped tapestries made up only about a third of all the pieces she recorded.
Almost every tapestry with adhesive residue in Ines's notebook was due to be shipped within a month, while pieces with later departure dates had been repaired only by stitching.
Almost every tapestry with adhesive residue in Ines's notebook had been repaired by the museum's newest staff members, while senior conservators' pieces had been repaired only by stitching.
g.explanation: 이네스의 의심은 "실크와 일정이 둘 다 불리할 때만" 접착제를 쓴다는 것, 즉 실크 날실과 임박한 출고일이라는 두 조건이 함께 있을 때만 쓴다는 것이다. A는 접착제가 두 조건을 모두 갖춘 작품에 몰려 있다는 점을 보여 준다. 또한 실크라도 출고일이 먼 작품은 바느질로만 수선됐다는 대조가 있어서, 실크만으로는 충분하지 않고 일정 압박도 필요하다는 점까지 확인해 준다. 그래서 가설을 가장 직접적으로 지지한다. B는 실크라는 변수 하나만 다룬다. 출고일에 대한 정보가 없어서 일정 압박이 필요하다는 부분을 뒷받침하지 못한다. C는 출고일이라는 변수 하나만 다룬다. 섬유 종류에 대한 정보가 없어서 울 작품에도 접착제를 썼을 가능성이 남는다. D는 지문에 없는 제3의 변수인 직원 경력을 끌어온다. 이는 이네스의 가설과 관련이 없다.
g.explanation_en: Ines suspects that her colleagues use the glue only when "the silk and the calendar are both against them." In other words, the tapestry must have silk warps AND be due to leave soon. Choice A supports this most directly. It shows that the adhesive appears on pieces that meet both conditions. It also shows that silk pieces with later departure dates were only stitched, so silk alone isn't enough; time pressure is needed too. Choice B looks only at fiber type. Without departure dates, it can't show that the deadline matters. Choice C looks only at departure dates. Without fiber information, it leaves open the possibility that quick-to-stitch wool pieces were glued too. Choice D brings in a third factor, staff experience, that Ines's suspicion never mentions, so it doesn't test her claim.
g.design: 정답이 되려면 지문 속 두 변수(섬유 종류와 출고 시점)를 함께 반영해야 한다. 오답은 각각 섬유만 본 결론(B), 출고 시점만 본 결론(C), 제3의 변수인 직원 경력으로 낸 결론(D)이며, 네 선택지 모두 같은 문장 틀로 썼다.

c.instruction: 지문에 상관관계나 동시 발생 사실만 제시하고, 이를 근거로 특정 가설(주장)의 인과성을 지지하는지 판단해야 하는 문항을 만들어라. 정답은 인과 방향과 대안 설명 가능성을 함께 고려해 타당하게 지지하는 것이어야 하고, 오답 3개는 각각 '상관을 그대로 인과로 오해', '인과 방향을 반대로 설정', '무관한 제3의 원인을 인과로 제시'로 구성하라.
c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A court stenographer records testimony that directly contradicts her employer's prior written summary submitted to the judge that morning

g.passage:
The following text is adapted from a novel. Ines Varga is a court stenographer whose employer, attorney Konrad Halvorsen, gave the judge a written summary of a witness's expected testimony that morning.

Ines's fingers kept moving even as the words landed. "The truck was already stopped when the light changed," the witness said. That was the opposite of what Halvorsen's summary claimed, the summary Ines herself had typed before dawn. She thought back to the noon recess: she had seen the witness at a corner table in the courthouse café across from Delia Marsh, counsel for the other side, the two of them leaning close over cold coffee. Now, keying the testimony line by line, Ines became convinced that whatever Marsh had said at that table was the reason the witness's story had changed.
g.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ines's suspicion?
options: Several people in the café that day saw the witness and Marsh talking for nearly the whole noon recess, and some noticed that the witness looked troubled when she returned to the courtroom.

In a recorded exchange with a bailiff shortly before the recess, the witness repeated the account in Halvorsen's summary, and no other source of new information about the accident reached her between that exchange and her testimony.
The witness had asked to meet Marsh at the café because, days earlier, she had privately come to doubt the account she originally gave Halvorsen.
The night before the trial, the witness studied newly released traffic-camera photographs of the intersection, and those photographs contradicted Halvorsen's summary.
g.explanation:
Ines는 증인이 점심시간에 상대측 변호인 Marsh와 만난 일과 증언이 바뀐 일이 함께 일어났다는 사실만 보고, 그 만남이 증언을 바꾼 원인이라고 추론한다. 이 인과 주장을 지지하려면 두 가지를 확인해야 한다. 증언이 정말 만남 이후에 바뀌었는지(인과 방향), 그리고 다른 원인이 없었는지(대안 설명)이다.
B(정답): 휴정 직전까지도 증인은 Halvorsen의 요약과 같은 진술을 했고, 그 뒤 증언하기 전까지 다른 새 정보를 접하지 않았다. 따라서 진술은 만남 이후에야 바뀌었고, 사이에 끼어든 다른 원인도 배제된다. 주장을 가장 직접적으로 지지한다.
A: 두 사람이 오래 대화했고 증인이 심란해 보였다는 내용은 둘이 함께 있었다는 동시 발생 사실을 다시 확인할 뿐이다. 상관을 인과로 착각하게 만드는 오답이다.
C: 증인이 이미 마음을 바꾼 상태에서 만남을 요청했다면, 증언 변화가 만남의 원인이 된다. 인과 방향이 거꾸로이므로 Ines의 추측을 오히려 약화한다.
D: 전날 밤 본 교통 카메라 사진이라는 제3의 원인이 증언 변화를 설명할 수 있다. 그러면 Marsh와의 만남은 원인이 아닐 수 있다.
g.explanation_en:
Ines sees two things happen together: the witness met opposing counsel Marsh at lunch, and her testimony changed. From that alone, she infers that the meeting caused the change. To support a causal claim like this, you need to know two things. First, did the change actually come after the meeting? Second, can other explanations be ruled out?
B (correct): Shortly before the recess, the witness still gave the account in Halvorsen's summary, and no other new information reached her before she testified. So the change came after the meeting, and no other cause could have stepped in between. This most directly supports Ines's suspicion.
A: Saying the two talked for a long time and the witness looked troubled only confirms that they were together. It treats correlation as causation.
C: If the witness had already changed her mind and then asked for the meeting, the change in her account caused the meeting, not the other way around. The causal direction is reversed, so this actually weakens Ines's suspicion.
D: The traffic-camera photographs she saw the night before are a third cause that could explain the change in testimony on their own. If so, the meeting with Marsh may not have been the cause at all.
g.design: The passage presents only a co-occurrence (a lunch meeting and changed testimony) and Ines's causal reading of it. The correct answer establishes the timing and rules out other causes. The three wrong answers restate the correlation, reverse the causal direction, or offer a third cause.

g.passage:
Text 1
In this excerpt from a short story, Marisol Vega, manager of a small branch library, reads a memo from the city office. It tells her to cut new purchases for the Spanish, Tagalog, and Vietnamese shelves and to put that money into English titles. Marisol folds the memo and thinks, almost with relief, that the order may not be so bad: if the shelves her patrons rely on grow thin, they will be pushed toward English books, and the push might speed their way into the life of the city.

Text 2
In this excerpt from the same story, Marisol watches Mr. Tran, who visits every Tuesday, run his finger along the Vietnamese shelf. He finds nothing he has not already read and leaves without borrowing anything. The next week he does not come. Over the following month, Marisol notices that several of the regulars from the Tagalog and Spanish sections have also stopped coming. Their library cards sit unused, and nobody takes out the English books she bought.
g.question: Based on the texts, how would the scene in Text 2 most likely bear on Marisol's reasoning in Text 1?
options: It would confirm that reasoning, since it shows patrons turning away from the shelves that had stopped offering them anything new.
It would complicate that reasoning, since it shows that patrons were reading more English books than Marisol had realized.
It would undercut that reasoning, since it shows that patrons stopped using the library altogether instead of switching to English books.
It would leave that reasoning untested, since it shows only what Mr. Tran did and nothing about the other patrons.
g.design: 정답은 Text 1의 예측(영어책으로 옮겨갈 것)과 Text 2의 결과(이용 자체 중단)를 연결해야 나온다. A는 '외면'이라는 표면적 일치로, D는 Mr. Tran에만 주목해 다른 단골 언급을 놓친 독해로 유도하는 오답이다.
g.explanation: Text 1에서 Marisol은 모국어 서가가 빈약해지면 이용자들이 영어책으로 옮겨가 도시 생활에 더 빨리 적응할 것이라고 예상한다. Text 2에서 이용자들은 도서관에 아예 오지 않고, 새로 산 영어책도 아무도 빌리지 않으므로 그 예상이 어긋난다. 따라서 정답은 C이다. A는 이용자들이 모국어 서가를 외면한 점은 맞지만, 그들이 영어책으로 옮겨가지 않았으므로 Marisol의 추론을 확인해 주지 않는다. B는 영어책을 아무도 빌리지 않았다는 내용과 반대이고, D는 다른 단골 여러 명도 발길을 끊었다는 서술을 놓쳤다.
g.explanation_en: In Text 1, Marisol predicts that if the home-language shelves grow thin, patrons will move to English books and fit into city life faster. Text 2 shows the opposite: patrons stop coming to the library at all, and nobody borrows the new English books. That undercuts her prediction, so the answer is C. A is right that patrons turned away from the depleted shelves, but they never switched to English books, so the scene doesn't confirm her reasoning. B contradicts the detail that no one checked out the English books, and D ignores the fact that several other regulars also stopped coming.

c.seed: an excerpt of literary fiction (novel/short story scene) — A painting restorer is instructed to apply techniques that artificially increase the perceived age and authenticity of a canvas to defraud buyers

g.passage:
Text 1
In the novel's opening chapter, the restorer Ilse Varga receives a small landscape from her employer with instructions to "give it a century." She bakes the varnish until fine cracks web the sky, rubs soot into the frame's grooves, and feels only the quiet pride of a craftsman. The narrator remarks that Ilse's hands, trained for thirty years, simply did what hands like hers had always done: they solved the problem placed in front of them, and the question of who would later buy the canvas never entered the workshop.

Text 2
A later chapter returns to the same workshop. Ilse has finished another "aged" canvas and, alone, holds a lamp close to the cracks she made. She notices that she has placed them exactly where a real crack would fall, following the strain of the stretcher bars. The precision unsettles her. Real age, she thinks, is careless; only someone who knows exactly whom she is fooling takes this much care. She sets the lamp down and does not pick up her brush again that night.
g.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the narrator's claim in Text 1 about Ilse's state of mind while working?
options: By agreeing that Ilse's long training lets her age canvases without thinking, and adding that this skill is what makes her employer value her
By agreeing that Ilse feels a craftsman's pride, and adding that her pride grows as her artificial cracks come to look more like real ones
By questioning whether Ilse's techniques are skilled enough to fool buyers, since real age leaves marks that are too careless to copy
By questioning whether Ilse really works with no thought of the buyer, since the care she takes suggests she knows her work is meant to deceive
g.explanation: Text 1의 서술자는 일세가 구매자를 전혀 생각하지 않고 장인으로서 문제만 해결했다고 말한다. Text 2는 일세가 균열을 지나치게 정확하게 배치한 것을 보고, 그런 정성은 누구를 속이는지 아는 사람만 들인다고 깨닫게 하므로 그 주장을 반박한다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. A와 B는 Text 1에 동의한다는 점에서 틀렸다. Text 2는 일세의 숙련도와 정확성을 인정하지만 그것을 자부심이 아니라 불안과 자각의 근거로 제시한다. C는 균열이 정확하다는 Text 2의 내용과 반대로 일세의 기술이 부족하다고 본다.
g.explanation_en: In Text 1, the narrator claims that Ilse works with nothing but a craftsman's pride and never thinks about who will buy the canvas. Text 2 pushes back on this: when Ilse sees how carefully she placed the cracks, she realizes that only someone who knows exactly whom she is fooling would take that much care. So D is correct. A and B are wrong because they agree with Text 1. Text 2 does acknowledge Ilse's skill and precision, but it treats them as a sign that she knows what she is doing, which unsettles her, not as a source of pride. C is wrong because Text 2 shows that her technique is very convincing, not too weak to fool buyers.
g.design: Two steps are needed: first identify the narrator's claim in Text 1 (Ilse doesn't think about buyers), then connect it to Text 2's point that her precision reveals she knows she is deceiving. A and B contain true details (her skill and precision) but make the wrong agree/disagree call. C has the right "questioning" frame but misreads what Text 2 says.

g.passage:
Text 1
In Dara Whitcomb's novel The Count, education coordinator Ines Ruiz watches a guard stack the week's algebra workbooks on a cart and wheel them back toward the property office twenty minutes before class. Ruiz concludes that the guard is acting alone, a petty man punishing her students out of personal spite, and she resolves to report him by name.

Text 2
A critic reviewing The Count notes that the novel quietly undercuts Ruiz's reading of the scene. Later chapters reveal a memo, signed by the warden's office months earlier, directing staff to "delay nonessential materials" whenever headcounts run long, an order the guard is simply carrying out as he was told. The workbooks vanish, the critic observes, because of a policy rather than a personality.
g.question: Based on the texts, how would the critic in Text 2 most likely respond to Ruiz's conclusion in Text 1?
options: By arguing that Ruiz is right that the workbooks are being withheld but wrong to put the blame on one guard's motives
By arguing that Ruiz is right to report the guard because the memo makes him responsible for following the warden's order
By arguing that Ruiz is wrong to think the workbooks are being withheld at all, since the guard is only moving them for a headcount
By arguing that Ruiz is right about the guard's spite but wrong to think that reporting him will help her students
g.explanation: Text 2의 비평가는 교재가 실제로 사라진다는 점("The workbooks vanish")은 인정하지만, 그 원인이 개인적 악의가 아니라 교도소장실의 정책이라고 본다. 따라서 Ruiz의 관찰은 맞고 원인 해석만 틀렸다고 반응할 것이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 메모를 언급하지만 비평가는 경비원을 책임자로 보지 않고 단지 지시를 따랐다고 하므로 틀리다. C는 headcount라는 지문 단어를 쓰지만 비평가는 교재가 보류된다는 사실 자체를 부정하지 않는다. D는 경비원의 악의를 인정하는데, 비평가는 바로 그 악의 해석을 부정한다.
g.explanation_en: The critic in Text 2 agrees that the workbooks really are being kept from the students ("The workbooks vanish"), but traces this to a policy from the warden's office, not to one man's spite. So the critic would say Ruiz has the facts right but the cause wrong, which is choice A. Choice B brings up the memo, but the critic says the guard is just following orders and never treats him as the one to blame. Choice C uses the word "headcount" from the text, but the critic never says the materials aren't being withheld. Choice D accepts that the guard is spiteful, and that's exactly the reading the critic rejects.
g.design: To pick the answer, you have to separate two parts of Ruiz's view: what she saw (accurate) and why she thinks it happened (wrong). Each wrong option gets something partly right, like the memo, the headcount, or "right but wrong" wording, and then flips the half that matters.

g.passage:
Text 1
In Teodora Vance's novel The Linen Floor, housekeeping supervisor Marisol Reyes notices a pattern while reviewing staffing charts late one night: rooms booked by guests with certain surnames consistently receive fewer attendants and shorter cleaning times. Vance presents this moment as a solitary revelation. The policy is buried so deeply in the hotel's scheduling software that only Marisol's unusual patience with numbers allows her to see what everyone else has missed.

Text 2
Readers often treat the spreadsheet scene in The Linen Floor as the novel's turning point, but Vance has carefully prepared for it. In earlier chapters, the room attendants joke bitterly about the "short-list floors," and an elderly attendant warns a new hire never to expect enough help on those rooms. When Marisol finally studies the charts, the numbers merely confirm what her staff have been telling her for months, in words she had chosen not to hear.
g.question: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the characterization of Marisol's late-night review in Text 1?
options: By agreeing that the policy is well hidden but arguing that the hotel's managers, rather than its software, are mainly responsible for concealing it
By arguing that the pattern Marisol finds had long been recognized by the room attendants, so her review is less an insight of her own than a delayed acceptance of their account
By arguing that the staffing pattern Marisol finds is more likely an accident of the scheduling software than a deliberate policy targeting particular guests
By agreeing that Marisol's skill with numbers is essential to the scene but arguing that the scene matters less than the confrontation that follows it
g.explanation: Text 1은 Marisol의 발견을 다른 모두가 놓친 것을 그녀 혼자 알아낸 '고독한 깨달음'으로 본다. Text 2는 객실 청소원들이 이미 'short-list floors'에 대해 말하고 있었고, 숫자는 그녀가 '듣지 않기로 했던' 내용을 확인했을 뿐이라고 하므로 B가 정답이다. A는 정책이 숨겨져 있다는 Text 1의 전제에 동의하는데, Text 2는 직원들이 이미 알고 있었다고 하므로 틀리다. C는 정책이 의도적이라는 점을 부정하는데, 두 글 어디에도 그런 근거가 없다. D는 이후의 대립 장면을 언급하지만 Text 2는 그런 장면을 다루지 않으며, Marisol의 능력이 핵심이라는 데 동의하지도 않는다.
g.explanation_en: Text 1 describes Marisol's discovery as a solitary revelation: she alone sees what everyone else has missed. Text 2 points out that the attendants already joked about the "short-list floors" and warned new hires, and it says the charts only confirmed what Marisol had "chosen not to hear." That makes B correct. A is wrong because it accepts Text 1's view that the policy is well hidden, while Text 2 says the staff already knew about it. C is wrong because neither text suggests the pattern is accidental. D is wrong because Text 2 never mentions a later confrontation, and it doesn't agree that Marisol's skill with numbers is what makes the scene work.
g.design: Text 2 never directly argues with Text 1. To choose B, students have to link the attendants' earlier comments to Text 2's point that the charts only confirmed what they had said. Choices A and D partly agree with Text 1, so students can rule them out only by comparing the two texts closely. Choice C is a reasonable-sounding reading that the texts do not support.
